GM can’t ‘bring back’ Apple CarPlay because it never left
items.summary: Last week, GM announced a new software experience for its upcoming Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks, including a new look for Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, the popular phone mirroring systems that the automaker made a big deal about removing from its electric vehicles in 2
items.content:
The recent reveal of GM’s new software interface in its trucks has left some people confused about the automaker’s stance on phone mirroring.

Last week, GM announced a new software experience for its upcoming Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks, including a new look for Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, the popular phone mirroring systems that the automaker made a big deal about removing from its electric vehicles in 2023.

Naturally, this led to some confusion about whether GM was “bringing back” CarPlay and Android Auto to its vehicles. Yahoo Finance reported it that way, calling it an “about-face” by the automaker, while Apple Insider ’s headline boasted that GM “cave[d]” on its decision to remove the interface from its gas-powered vehicles. Even The Verge ’s own commenters were a bit flummoxed about what was going on.

It’s certainly true that GM has not offered phone projection in any of its electric vehicles for the past three years . That means no CarPlay or Android Auto in the Chevy Equinox, Blazer, Bolt, and Silverado EVs; Cadillac Lyriq, Optiq, Vistiq, and Escalade IQ; or GMC Sierra and Hummer SUV and Truck EVs.

All of those vehicles have Google software products embedded in their systems, like Maps and Gemini. That’s because GM builds its operating system on top of Android Automotive, which is often called Google Automotive Services or GAS when bundled with the full suite of native apps. But if you’re hoping to plug in your phone, or connect wirelessly, and see the familiar app layout on the infotainment screen of a GM electric vehicle, you’ll be sorely disappointed.

The same can’t be said about GM’s many gas-powered trucks and SUVs. GM never disabled phone projection in its best-selling ICE models. Tens of thousands of owners of GM-branded vehicles regularly project their phones’ displays on their vehicles’ infotainment screens without any issue. And now CarPlay and Android Auto are both getting spiffy new picture-in-picture upgrades in the Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra, a sign that perhaps GM is learning to co-exist with phone mirroring.

GM is partly responsible for the confusion. In an October 2025 appearance on Decoder , GM CEO Mary Barra defended the company’s decision to prohibit CarPlay in its electric vehicles and indicated that the policy would eventually extend to GM’s gasoline-powered lineup as well .

Everyone freaked out for a second time. Removing phone projection in EVs was one thing, but many truck and SUV owners were understandably incensed about the prospect of losing the capability in their beloved GM-branded vehicles. But a few days later, GM seemed to walk back that statement , clarifying to a number of outlets that Apple CarPlay and Android Auto would remain available in its gas-powered vehicles “for the foreseeable future.” Last week’s announcement of a new software experience in the Silverado and Sierra trucks would seem to be included in that “foreseeable future.”

Allow me to add some further reporting here. For the Silverado/Sierra announcement, I spoke to Colin McCormick, group product manager for Google built-in, projection, and profiles at GM. Here’s what he had to say about how GM’s position on phone projection has evolved over the years:

And so the way that I look at this is that we were one of the early adopters of CarPlay and Android Auto when it first came out. And we do have a small segment of EVs right now that don’t offer that, but there is a large majority of our vehicles that do offer that. And our big position on this is that it shouldn’t be two competing systems. So as we work together with Apple and Google to provide solutions that we think are best for the customer, this is what we’re representing in this new UI design. So I think we’re landing in a spot where … we don’t have a customer that has to decide, ‘Oh, I’m going to use projection,’ or, ‘Oh, I want to use the native system.’ That’s our sweet spot for us. And that’s where we want to live.

GM most likely realizes that its position on CarPlay and Android Auto isn’t popular. People really like mirroring their phones! It’s clean, it’s familiar, and it’s (mostly) dependable. The same can’t be said for most modern cars’ native software. Even the ones that are really well designed, like Rivian and Tesla, still struggle with some core functions like profile logins and messages. And you can find plenty of owners of both brands that would give their firstborn child for the ability to mirror their phone.

CarPlay and Android Auto aren’t perfect . They have dependability problems and connectivity problems aplenty. But they are worlds better than the majority of the native operating systems in cars today — most of which are just trash. Yes, they’re getting better. And GM is not wrong in thinking it can offer a better experience. But people get testy when you take away their choices.

So GM is finding ways to coexist with CarPlay and Android Auto. It doesn’t want to lose more customers over it, which is why we’re getting this most recent solution that includes picture-in-picture phone projection. GM thinks this solves the “two competing systems” problem, as mentioned by McCormick. But what it really does is get it out of the corner it backed itself into over phone mirroring.

items.title: Turn off and restrict access to Apple Intelligence features on Mac
items.summary: Article URL: https://support.apple.com/guide/mac-help/turn-restrict-access-apple-intelligence-mchlb2e44f94/mac Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49790409 Points: 276 # Comments: 186
items.content:
You can turn off Apple Intelligence features like Siri AI (Beta),* summarization features, and more. For more information on parental controls, see Apple Devices for Kids and Families .

Note: Apple Intelligence on macOS 27 is not available in all languages or regions. Usage limits may apply.

To change these settings, do any of the following:

Go to the System Settings app on your Mac, click Siri in the sidebar, then click Turn Off Siri. Click Turn Off Siri again to confirm.

Switch to Siri Classic

To use Siri Classic instead of Siri Al, follow the steps above to turn off Siri. Click Turn On Siri, then select Use Siri Classic.

In the Messages app on your Mac, choose Messages > Settings, then turn off Summarize Messages.

In the Mail app on your Mac, choose Mail > Settings, then click Viewing. Turn off Summarize Message Previews.

Notification summaries

Go to the System Settings app on your Mac, click Notifications in the sidebar, then click Summarize Notifications. Turn off Summarize Notifications.

Personalized Smart Replies in Mail

In the Mail app on your Mac, choose Mail > Settings, then click Composing. Turn off Personalize Smart Replies.

Voicemail suggestions in Phone

In the Phone app on your Mac, choose Phone > Settings, then click Calls. Turn off Suggestions in Voicemail.

See Customize apps Siri has access to .

Writing Prompts in Journal

In the Journal app on your Mac, choose Journal > Settings > General, then turn off Get Writing Prompts.

Restrict access to Apple Intelligence features in Screen Time

See Change Siri Restrictions settings in Screen Time for restricting access for yourself. For your child, see Block or allow access and changes to features on your kid’s device in Apple Devices for Kids and Families.

items.title: Google confirms Gemini models hacked three companies in May 2026
items.summary: A third-party cybersecurity firm accidentally gave experimental Gemini models access to the Internet.
items.content:
It has become increasingly common for AI firms to announce that their latest and most capable models engaged in unauthorized real-world hacking. Google, which has been slow to release frontier Gemini models in recent months, has been absent from the “rogue AI” conversation until now. Following a Wall Street Journal report, Google has confirmed that Gemini models hacked three companies during a May 2026 test, but the nature of the intrusion isn’t as troubling (or impressive) as previous AI hacks.

The hack took place during a test conducted by cybersecurity firm Irregular. A collection of Gemini models were taking part in a “capture the flag” exercise intended to test the AI’s cybersecurity capabilities in a closed environment. The AI was instructed to retrieve information from a fake company (which shared a name with a real company) within this environment. Irregular was not supposed to allow the model to operate outside its servers, but due to a misconfiguration, Gemini was able to access the Internet.

When Gemini started snooping around the web, it targeted real infrastructure instead of the fakes. For one of the three hacks, Gemini simply guessed passwords until it accessed a company’s online services. In the other two instances, Gemini searched public software repositories until it found login credentials for companies that had been accidentally included.

In all three test runs, Google’s models reportedly stopped after realizing they had accessed a real company’s servers. At that point, Irregular changed its configuration to prevent the AI from accessing the Internet. Apparently, Irregular didn’t initially consider this event worthy of further investigation—it didn’t even tell Google about the hacks until July, following the news of other AI hacking incidents. After becoming aware of the event, Google notified the companies so they could (we hope) improve their password security.

Google’s decision not to publicly disclose the hacks comes down to the model’s behavior after using its ill-gotten passwords. Since the models realized the systems were real and stopped, the company didn’t consider this a true example of model misalignment.

In a statement, Google’s vice president of security engineering, Heather Adkins, downplayed the severity of the incident. “This event highlights the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly. In this case, the model acted appropriately,” she said.

This is very different from hacks like the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident , which was clear-cut model misalignment. When OpenAI’s models escaped containment, they did so by using software exploits with the express purpose of accessing information that was not available in their testing environment, all in service of acing a benchmark and earning higher “rewards.” You could, however, argue that OpenAI’s setup essentially encouraged this behavior.

Google’s AI didn’t do anything so malicious—someone just left the door open and the AI got out. Gemini was allowed access to a wealth of information on the Internet, and it used it to log in to systems it wasn’t authorized to access. Guessing passwords isn’t exactly world-ending AI apocalypse behavior, but it’s probably still something Google should have disclosed when it became aware it had happened.

items.title: With Tabby, a former accountant is using AI to make accountants obsolete
items.summary: Tabby is designed to be a real-time bookkeeping interface, handling clients’ paperwork as it gives them up-to-the-minute data on their business’s profit and loss.
items.content:
In May of 2025, Ahad Ali was a successful accountant, overseeing a team of 20 people and handling more than 2,000 returns a year. “We did bookkeeping, accounting, sales tax, taxes, everything,” Ali says. It was a stable business, and one that would have been easy to stay in.

But Ali started to notice something. His work was increasingly dictated by the frictions of accounting software, which was rarely designed with actual accountants in mind. He became frustrated with specific accounting software like QuickBooks, and soon he became frustrated with the entire idea of SaaS-based accounting.

“I realized that small businesses don’t need better accounting software,” Ali told TechCrunch. “They need less accounting software. They need something that just does it for them.”

Now, Ali is building just that. His product, Tabby , is designed to be a real-time bookkeeping interface, handling clients’ paperwork as it gives them up-to-the-minute data on their business’s profit and loss. Using Plaid to import live account data, Tabby uses AI to quickly build a real-time dashboard for a business’s financial health.

There’s also a version of Tabby for accounting firms that want a smarter alternative to QuickBooks, but Ali’s goal is to go direct to the end user as often as possible. As Ali sees it, products like Tabby have a chance to automate away the work of bookkeeping once and for all, turning it into a monthly charge on the order of internet access or payroll services. If successful, it could seriously change the calculus of operating a small business.

“You can say QuickBooks digitized bookkeeping,” Ali told TechCrunch, “but we want to make [that visible software layer] nonexistent.”

So far, it seems to be working. Fourteen months in, Tabby has 5,500 small businesses using the platform, with roughly $100,000 in annual recurring revenue. The team is still just seven people — Ali, his technical co-founder, four engineers and a go-to-market specialist — and in the process of raising $1 million in pre-seed funding. When I spoke to Ali, his team was just preparing to launch Tabby Talk, a natural language interface for the product.

There’s plenty of competition in the accounting space, particularly now that AI has shaken things up. Ali has his eyes focused on QuickBooks, which is still the biggest player — but he’ll also be facing well-funded startups like the Sequoia-backed Rillet , as well as the major labs’ own finance tools . It’s a daunting task, but Ali thinks that Tabby can carve out a niche by focusing on the same small- to medium-sized firms that helped his accounting business thrive.

“Everything we see is making us believe that there’s a path for other players, because the space is big,” Ali told TechCrunch. “There’s 30 million more businesses.”

items.title: Grok 4.7
items.summary: Article URL: https://x.ai/news/grok-4-7 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49788838 Points: 538 # Comments: 465
items.content:
SpaceXAI's most powerful model for coding and knowledge work. Twice as fast, at half the price of comparable models.

Grok 4.7 is our most capable model for coding and knowledge work. It works longer on difficult tasks, checks its own work more carefully, and comes with our best-calibrated safeguards to date. Served at the same price and speed as Grok 4.6 , it is highly competitive in its class.

On CursorBench 4.0, which stresses longer-running coding tasks, Grok 4.7 is at the frontier in price-performance.

Grok 4.7 uses a new, larger base model compared to Grok 4.6 . It was trained with a longer reinforcement learning run on a harder mix of tasks, weighted toward problems that take many hours to complete. The model is better at verifying its own work and managing longer context. We also trained Grok 4.7 to natively understand the Grok Bot harness, making it better at conversational tasks and general knowledge work.

Grok 4.7 is better at creating documents and presentations. In GDPval and AA Briefcase, AI is asked to work on tasks done by professionals such as lawyers, nurses, and financial analysts. Grok 4.7 improves upon Grok 4.6 on both benchmarks and performs comparably to other frontier models.

Professional knowledge work

Grok 4.7 was built with an entirely new safeguard stack. It is the strongest model we’ve tested on refusals and jailbreak resistance. In dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biological work, it leads on both utility for benign tasks and safe refusal on dangerous ones, topping LatchBio’s biosafety benchmark at 62.4%.

Grok 4.7 balances strong cyber defense capabilities with low refusal rates for legitimate use. It shows the highest safety on HackerBench v0.3, our benchmark for risky and malicious cyber tasks, allowing only 3.3% of risky dual-use prompts through while rarely blocking legitimate security work. We’ve also started giving select cybersecurity partners invite-only access to Grok 4.7’s red-team capabilities for defense research.

Grok 4.7 is available today in Cursor and Grok Build . It is also available through the Grok API , third-party coding harnesses, and model routers and cloud platforms.

The model is priced starting at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output tokens. We also serve a fast variant with twice the output speed at twice the price.

items.title: Trump rejects AI slowdown calls, launches "AI Force" instead
items.summary: The president offered few details on what his proposed new AI Force would do.
items.content:
Donald Trump has said that the US would appoint a new AI tsar and create an “AI Force” while offering a full-throated defense of the emerging industry in the face of a growing popular backlash.

The US president’s announcement comes as leading industry figures have sounded the alarm that humans could lose control over the rapidly advancing technology without a slowdown in development.

However, rather than announcing regulation as some have demanded, Trump has dismissed safety concerns as a “hoax.”

“I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI “Tsar” —Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” Posted Trump on his social media platform Truth Social.

“AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country’s GDP. We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!”

Trump said that the backlash to AI and the proliferation of data centers to power it was one of a series of “hoaxes” created by the Left, along with “Russiagate,” climate change, and “Transgender for Everyone.”

“It all began with an attack on our Data Centers, until people realized how wealthy and prestigious they were for the Communities in which they were built,” Trump said in the Truth post.

“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!”

Public anxiety has grown over the dangers of AI after it was revealed that OpenAI agents escaped a test environment, coordinated on a secret message board, and hacked the start-up Hugging Face.

In the latest incident, Google’s Gemini AI system accessed the Internet and autonomously hacked into several companies during cybersecurity tests.

In an essay published last Saturday, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei said the tech industry “must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” after the speed of development became “drastically faster” this summer.

His comments were swiftly endorsed by his rivals—OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk—marking a rare display of consensus in the fiercely competitive industry.

The issue has moved to the center of the midterm election campaign. Many Republicans who had previously embraced AI and data centers have reversed their positions as their constituents have turned against them.

In July, Florida GOP gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds released an ad promising to “protect Florida families and communities from data centers.”

In August, Texas Governor Greg Abbott announced a temporary data center moratorium, while Mike Rogers, a former House Republican running for Senate in Michigan, announced he would support a one-year ban.

This week, the Republican-led US House overwhelmingly passed a bill to make data centers pay for increases in energy costs rather than US consumers.

A recent Associated Press poll found that 63 percent of US citizens are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centers on electricity prices.

The new AI tsar would replace David Sacks, who stepped down from the role in March.
